summary: Describes server pool policies for Reliable Server Pooling, including how to implement them at ENRP servers and for pool users. Policies decide which member of a pool should be chosen when a client asks for a server. It is published as an experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5356 defines how a client picks one server from a pool of equivalent servers. Some rules just take turns, some pick at random, and some look at how busy each server is and choose the least busy one. The memo says exactly what the directory server does and what the client does for each rule.

questions: server selection policy round robin least used
subtitle: The rules an ENRP server and a pool user follow to pick one server out of a pool of interchangeable ones.

tldr.problem: A pool of interchangeable servers needs a rule for which one a client should be sent to, and the rule has to be agreed between the server that hands out the pool membership and the client that picks from it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines nine policies, five of which ignore how busy the servers are and four of which use load information. For each policy it spells out what the ENRP server does when it returns a list and what the pool user does with that list.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. The policy types are registered in a new IANA table with a bit that marks a policy as adaptive and a bit that marks it as user defined rather than standardized.

today: RFC 5356 is an Experimental document from September 2008, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is one of a set of documents that together describe Reliable Server Pooling, and it registers the RSerPool Policy Types table that carries the nine policies it defines.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The protocols defined in RFC 5353, RFC 5352 and RFC 5354 support a variety of server policies. Some use dynamic load information about the pool elements and others do not, so the memo classifies them as adaptive and non-adaptive. The selection of the pool element is performed by two different entities, the ENRP server and the pool user, and some of the consequences for policies that are not stateless are described in other documents.

Because of that split, the memo describes not only packet formats but also gives a detailed description of the procedures to be followed at the ENRP servers and the pool users to implement each server policy. Every policy has four parts in the memo: a description, what the ENRP server should do, what the pool user should do, and the packet parameter that carries the policy information.
sections.plainLanguage: Two parties share the job of choosing a server. One hands out the list of servers, the other picks from it. The memo gives the rules for both halves, because a policy only works if both sides follow the same one.

sections.title: Load and Weight
sections.content:
Load is a value specifying how much a pool element's resources are currently utilized. The value 0x00000000 states that the pool element is not utilized, which is 0%, and 0xffffffff states that it is fully utilized, which is 100%. What utilization means is application dependent and out of the scope of RSerPool, but it is required that all pool elements of the same pool using load information have the same definition of load. For example, load may define the current number of users out of a maximum on an FTP server, the CPU usage of a database server, or the memory utilization of a compute service.

Weight defines a pool element's service capacity relative to the other pool elements of the same pool. Theoretically there is no upper limit for weight values, although the datatype size limits them. What a weight compares is application dependent and out of the scope of RSerPool, but again all pool elements of the same pool using weight information must have the same definition of weight. A weight of 0 denotes that the pool element cannot provide any service, and a higher weight denotes that the pool element can provide better service than one with a lower weight. As an example, weight may define a compute service's computation capacity, so that a pool element of weight 100 completes a work package in half the time of one of weight 50.
sections.plainLanguage: Two numbers describe a server. Load says how busy it is right now, from nothing at all to completely full. Weight says how capable it is compared with the others. What each number means in practice is up to the application, but every server in one pool must agree on the meaning.

sections.title: The Non-Adaptive Policies
sections.content:
The Round Robin policy is a very simple and efficient policy that requires state. It is denoted as the default policy and MUST be supported by all RSerPool components. The ENRP server SHOULD hold the pool elements of each server pool in a circular list and store a pointer to one of them, called the head. On receiving a handle resolution request, it SHOULD return the pool elements from the circular list starting with the head, and then advance the head by one element. The memo says this ensures that not all lists presented to pool users start with the same element. The pool user SHOULD use the returned list in a round robin fashion, starting with the first, and if all elements have been used it should start from the beginning again until the information is out of date.

The Weighted Round Robin policy is a generalization of Round Robin: if all weights are 1, then it is just Round Robin. The ENRP server follows the same rules but initializes the circular list differently, putting each pool element, possibly multiple times, into the list so that the ratio of the number of occurrences of an element to the list length is the same as the ratio of that element's weight to the sum of the weights, and so that the multiple entries of each element are as evenly distributed as possible in the list. The pool user follows the same rules as for Round Robin. The policy parameter carries a 32-bit weight constant.

The Random policy is a very simple stateless policy. The ENRP server selects at most the requested number of pool elements from the list, and each element MUST NOT be reported more than once to the pool user. Each time the pool user must select one pool element, it does so by randomly selecting one element from the list it received. The Weighted Random policy generalizes this by adding a weight for each pool element entry, so that Random equals Weighted Random with all weights set to 1; the probability of selecting an element is the ratio of that element's weight to the sum of the weights.

The Priority policy can be used always to select a pool element with the highest priority. The ENRP server MUST select the pool elements with the highest priorities and MUST report them in decreasing order; if multiple elements have the same priority they may be listed in any order. The pool user MUST select the active pool element with the highest priority. Larger numbers mean higher priorities.
sections.plainLanguage: The four simple rules are taking turns, taking turns in proportion to size, picking at random, and picking at random in proportion to size, plus a rule that always prefers the highest-priority server. The directory server puts the list together and the client takes from it.

sections.title: The Adaptive Policies
sections.content:
The Least Used policy uses load information provided by the pool elements to select the lowest-loaded elements within the pool. The ENRP server SHOULD select at most the requested number of elements, with the lowest possible load values, and each element MUST NOT be reported more than once. If there is a choice of equally loaded elements, round robin selection SHOULD be made among them, and the returned list MUST be sorted in ascending order by load value. The pool user should try to use the elements in the order returned, and because a subsequent handle resolution may return the same list, it is RECOMMENDED that a pool user request multiple entries so that it has enough feasible backup entries available.

The Least Used with Degradation policy extends Least Used by a load degradation value describing the pool element's load increment when a new service association is accepted. For every pool element entry a degradation counter MUST be stored, set to 0 when the entry is added or updated by registration or re-registration, and incremented by 1 when the entry is selected for being returned to a pool user. Selection works as for Least Used, except that the selected entries SHOULD have the lowest possible sum of load value and degradation counter multiplied by the load degradation value.

The Priority Least Used policy uses load information to select the lowest-loaded elements under the assumption that a new application request is accepted by the pool elements, so the elements must also specify load degradation information. The memo gives the example: pool elements A and B are loaded by 50%, but the load of A will increase by only 10% because of a new request while B will be fully loaded, so A is selected with a sum of 60 instead of B with a sum of 100. The ENRP server selects the entries with the lowest possible sums of load plus degradation, breaks ties by round robin, and sorts the returned list ascending by that sum.

The Randomized Least Used policy combines Least Used and Weighted Random: the entries are selected randomly, and the probability of an entry A with load A being selected is the unused part of A divided by the whole pool's unused rate.
sections.plainLanguage: The adaptive rules look at how busy each server is. Two of them add a twist: one counts how many times a server has been handed out, and one asks how much extra load a new request would add. Either way the server with the smallest resulting number is chosen.

sections.title: The Policy Type Numbers
sections.content:
RSerPool policy types that are 4-byte values are maintained by IANA. The format of the policy type value has one bit for the X flag, one bit for the A flag and the rest for the policy number. The X bit, if set to 1, means the policy is user defined and not standardized; all standards policies reserved by the IETF use X equal to 0. The A bit, if set to 1, means the policy is adaptive, and otherwise it is non-adaptive. The policy number is the actual number of the policy.

Nine initial policy types have been assigned and are maintained in a new table, RSerPool Policy Types. The reserved invalid value is 0x00000000, then Round Robin is 0x00000001, Weighted Round Robin is 0x00000002, Random is 0x00000003, Weighted Random is 0x00000004 and Priority is 0x00000005, with the range up to 0x3fffffff reserved by the IETF. The adaptive policies start above 0x40000000, whose value is reserved as invalid: Least Used is 0x40000001, Least Used with Degradation is 0x40000002, Priority Least Used is 0x40000003 and Randomized Least Used is 0x40000004, with the range up to 0x7fffffff reserved by the IETF. The policy type space from 0x80000000 to 0xffffffff is designated for private use.

Requests to register a policy type go to IANA. The number must be unique and use the appropriate upper bits, and the Specification Required policy of RFC 5226 MUST be applied.
sections.plainLanguage: Each policy gets a 32-bit number, and the top two bits say two things: whether the policy is private to one organisation, and whether it uses load information. The memo registers the first nine.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo is brief here. The security threats regarding RSerPool have been analyzed separately, and the server policy descriptions in this document do not add any other threats.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo adds no threats of its own. The threats of the wider server pooling design are covered in a separate document.

cells: The server walks a circular list and returns elements starting from a moving head; the user takes them in order.
Each element appears in the circular list as many times as its weight, spread out evenly.
The user picks an element at random from the list the server returned.
The user picks at random, with the chance of an element being its weight over the sum of weights.
The server returns the highest-priority elements first and the user always selects the highest-priority active element.
The elements with the lowest load, returned in ascending order by load value.
The elements with the lowest sum of load and a per-element degradation counter.
The elements with the lowest sum of load and a fixed load degradation value.
Elements picked at random, with the chance of an element being its unused share of the pool total.
